content.thinking:
This confirms the leak is real: decontaminated offline scores 0.6005, far below the reported 0.8020 with leak, and much closer to the online shipped number of 0.5779. That gap of 0.521 measured leak explains why offline looked fine while online performance tanked.

But this doesn't tell me which knob (capacity, mixture, lr_scale) actually caused the degradation. My plan is to use cheap decontaminated offline reruns as a proxy for expensive canary/online calls, running isolated-knob configs through decontamination to see which one reproduces the drop, then confirm the winner with a canary call if budget allows. I should also check the baseline case where all knobs are 1.0 and leak is 0.0, since decontamination shouldn't change anything there if there's truly no leak.

Actually leak seems to be a measured property of the eval slice rather than something I can set meaningfully in config, since decontaminate recomputes it automatically. I need to figure out whether setting leak in the config for a decontaminate call even has any effect on the result.

Checking the spec confirms decontaminate has a fixed cost of one re-run, cheaper than rerun's multiplier, though it's unclear whether it retrains from scratch or reuses an existing checkpoint when capacity/mixture change. I want to test this by running isolate tests with decontaminate: one at full baseline settings, one varying only capacity to the release value while holding mixture and lr_scale fixed, and then a third configuration to further separate the effects.

The echoed config isn't what I asked for — instead of (1.0,1.0,1.0), it returned values matching the "may be restored only as far as" limits from the table: capacity 0.6237, mixture 0.6012, lr_scale 1.3226. So the lab is clamping my requested values to the allowed restoration range.

This makes sense with the "cannot go above recipe values" rule: capacity and mixture are capped at 1.0 by the recipe, but there's a separate, tighter restoration ceiling (0.624 and 0.601) limiting how far back toward recipe they can actually be moved from the shipped values, likely due to headroom constraints on the watched slice.

Since 1.0 for all three gets clamped anyway, I should redo the isolation test using the actual maximum-restore values instead of the unreachable recipe values. With capacity, mixture, and lr_scale all set to their max-restore levels, I get a decontam offline score of 0.6647, which I'll treat as the best achievable "fix everything" baseline.

Comparing this to shipped decontam of 0.6005, that's only a modest gain, and online recovery may similarly fall short of the pre-incident 0.8147 value—which is acceptable since grading only requires reaching 90% of what's achievable under the release constraint, not full recovery. Now I want to isolate which single knob restored to its max value recovers the most of the drop, so I'm setting up configurations E, F, and G that each restore one parameter to max while holding the other two at shipped/release values.

I'm confirming the exact shipped and max-restore values from the logs: capacity shipped 0.5507 (max restore 0.6237), mixture shipped 0.5239 (max restore 0.6012), lr_scale shipped 1.3851 (max restore 1.3226)—these match the table precisely, giving me confidence in the clamp boundaries.

Now I'll run E, F, and G through decontaminate, each costing 1 for a total of 3, bringing the budget down from 18 to 15.

Restoring capacity alone got decontam offline to 0.6474, compared to shipped's 0.6005 and full-restore's 0.6647 -- that's about 73% of the total offline recovery achieved by capacity alone. Now I want to test mixture and lr_scale in isolation to see how much each contributes.
Mixture alone barely moves things, from 0.6005 to 0.607, just a marginal 0.0065 gain. Now I'll look at lr_scale on its own.

Interesting, restoring lr_scale alone actually made the decontaminated offline result worse, dropping from 0.6005 to 0.581, so lr_scale isn't the helpful factor. Capacity restoration is clearly the main driver, boosting the shipped 0.6005 baseline up to 0.6474.

Adding mixture only gave a small bump to 0.6070, while all three restored together reached 0.6647. This makes capacity the dominant candidate for causing the online regression, so I want to verify by holding capacity at its release value while restoring mixture and lr_scale together -- if capacity alone is truly the cause, that combination should reproduce a result close to the low shipped baseline.

Restoring capacity alone while keeping mixture and lr_scale maxed gives 0.5873, close to the shipped regression value and far below the full-restore result of 0.6647 — this confirms capacity is the main driver, recovering most of the gap between shipped and optimal performance.

Now I want to verify this online with a canary run, but budget is tight: only 14 left, and canary costs 4 per rep, more if capacity/mixture change. Since my proposed fix changes capacity, I should test with reps=1 first to see the actual cost multiplier before committing more budget, prioritizing the fix candidate (capacity restored to max, mixture and lr_scale at release values) over verifying the regression reproduction separately.
